title: East/WOI gets its title shot back but will be shorthanded - Democrat and Chronicle
content: The door is open for the East High/World of Inquiry football team to play in the Section V Class B championship game Nov. 14, after a ruling by a state athletic association and a Section V official to reinstate the Eagles into the high school tournament. East High/World of Inquiry won a semifinal game at Monroe, 14-6, last Saturday. But seconds after a tackle on the final play of the elimination game Nov. 7, players from both teams began fighting on the field, including those who were on the sidelines. Officials at both schools said they were notified later that day each team was disqualified from the tournament. The decision was made this week and announced Nov. 11 to allow East/World of Inquiry to play Honeoye Falls-Lima, 3 p.m. Saturday at Saint John Fisher University. "I was very optimistic that they were going to find out who was involved and who was not involved," East High/World of Inquiry coach James Vann said. "Hope was still alive. We kept it business as usual (by practicing leading up to a game). "I knew they were going to do their due diligence." Rochester City School District superintendent Eric Jay Rosser said in a statement earlier this week he "along with District leadership, have been personally engaged in ongoing discussions with leaders from Section V and the New York State Public High School Athletic Association to address the disqualification of our student-athletes and advocate for those who were not involved in the incident." Section V executive director Kathy Hoyt, at the time of publication, had not returned phone calls made to her on Veterans Day, a federal holiday. "We feel like we did what we needed to do, provide the information," East High athletic director Eric Robinson said. "The incident was unfortunate. I would never bad-mouth Monroe, we've worked together, we're going to work together. "There was something that got out of hand, sparked in the spur of the moment. We don't feel like we were given a break. We provided the information that it wasn't a widespread thing. Our whole team should not have been suspended." The Eagles are going to play without 14 players, including 10 members of their starting lineups on Saturday, leaving the team "probably short four or five on each unit, offensively and defensively," according to Robinson. The East High athletic director said a group that included Rochester City School District officials, the Monroe athletic director and East High/WOI assistant coaches came together and watched a "painstaking amount" of footage of the incident. There were media clips, security camera footage, football scouting services video and recordings from phones owned by spectators. Then a list of East High/WOI players to suspend for the championship game was sent to Section V. "We basically went player by player, started from uniform No. 0 and watched each kid and their course of action," Robinson said. "Fourteen of them got into the melee or squared up like they wanted to. "If they had to be held back, we took them out (of consideration to play). I think the section was happy with how thorough it was. It showed we conceded that we had players involved. It showed that we were honest. That's why I put together a group that wasn't just East. We weren't trying to sandbag or hide kids." Robinson also said, "I give Kathy Hoyt credit (along with a NYSPHSAA official), they listened. They reviewed the video. That's why it was taking so long. "They gave us the opportunity to prove that everyone definitely was not involved, that we weren't trying to hide anything." The East High/World of Inquiry Eagles (7-2) are one of the top football teams in Section V, and are No. 4 in the Class B state rankings. Honeoye Falls-Lima (7-3) entered the same state rankings this week at No. 25. The Cougars could have been awarded the second Section V Football Championship in team history, if the disqualification of East High/WOI remained. "We can only play who they tell us to play," HF-L coach John Russ said. "We are going to give it our best shot and see what happens.” Russ said he expected to receive an updated East High/World of Inquiry roster by 3 p.m. Nov. 11. "At the end of the day, it goes to Section V and NYSPHSAA," Russ said. "They have to figure which ones can play and what are the consequences. “If they feel like (the decision) is accurate and in the best interest of East High/World of Inquiry, that's what we have to go with." Any disqualified player must sit out the equivalent of two halves or 24 scoreboard minutes, before becoming eligible to play again. "I'm not looking ahead, HF-L is a good team," Vann said. "We played them last year and they were up 14-0." James Johnson, who grew up in the city of Rochester and is a graduate of Edison Tech in the Rochester City School District, has worked as a full-time journalist covering high school sports for the Democrat and Chronicle since 1996. title: Anne V. Ayres Obituary - Press & Sun-Bulletin - Press & Sun-Bulletin
content: Anne V. Ayres joined the heavenly angels on October 26, 2026, at the age of 102. She was predeceased by her husband, Dr. John P. Ayres; parents, Anthony Kritkausky and Anna (Krasauskas) Kritkausky; siblings, Dr. Anthony Kritkausky, Violet Shirhall and Stephanie Laszewski and their spouses; and several nieces and nephews. The youngest child of Lithuanian immigrants, Anne's formative years were a blend of Old World traditions and New World ways. She was an avid reader and a creative spirit, finding expression in her arts and crafts. She became an accomplished seamstress, gardener and needlepointer and had a natural gift for drafting and decorating. Anne graduated from Binghamton Central High School and the Charles S. Wilson School of Nursing in 1945 as a registered nurse. Through the newly formed US Cadet Nurse Corps, she completed her nursing education on a full scholarship. As part of her training, she was assigned to Halloran General Hospital, the nation's largest Army hospital during WWII. Anne obtained advanced certification in public health from the University of Michigan, returning to Binghamton to work for the city as a public health nurse. There, she met City Veterinarian John P. Ayres. They married in 1951. The two built an active veterinary practice, first in Corbettsville and then on Binghamton's Southside. In later years, they established a private mortgage financing business, helping many local families with the purchase of their first homes. She served as a PTA and Children's Daycare board member; Girl Scout leader and Phelps Mansion Museum docent among other volunteer activities. Anne was a loving person filled with grace, kindness and generosity and an unwavering devotion to family and friends. She never spoke harshly of anyone and made everyone feel welcome and loved. She raised her children, cared for her elderly father, worked alongside her husband, made home-cooked meals nightly and volunteered, all the while creating precious memories for her family at their Zane Road home and their cottage on Tripp Lake. Her happiest moments were at the lake where generations gathered and countless family memories were made. She was one of the last of a remarkable era, a connection to the past for many and a living example of society's most respected values to all who knew her. Anne is survived by her children, Christine Ayres (Robert Schultheisz) and Dr. John R. Ayres (Deborah); grandchildren Carly Ayres (Sebastian Speier) and Ellyn Farrar (Ryan); great-grandchild Matisse Speier; step-grandchildren Michael Schultheisz (Heather), Robert Schultheisz (Maggie) and Heidi Campbell (Kevin) and their children, Aaron, Ashton, Nathan, Brooke, Isabelle and Connor; and numerous beloved nieces and nephews. At her request, her body was donated to SUNY Upstate Medical University, Syracuse. The family will receive friends on Saturday, November 21, at 11:00 AM at Saints John and Andrew Catholic Church, 1263 Vestal Ave., Binghamton. Mass will follow at 12:00. title: Robert V. "Bob" Wirtz Obituary - Mitchell Funeral Homes
content: Robert V. "Bob" Wirtz, age 94, of Chelsea, MI, passed away on November 10, 2026 at Legacy Assisted Living in Jackson, MI. Bob was born on March 11, 1932 in Detroit, MI, the son of Lionel and Catharine (Bueke) Wirtz. He graduated from East Detroit High School and shortly thereafter began working for Chrysler at the Mound Road Truck Assembly Plant. He enlisted in the United States Air Force with the 86th Fighter-Interceptor Wing. He served as an airplane mechanic aboard an aircraft carrier during the Korean War. He departed from San Francisco in 1952, sailing under the Golden Gate Bridge enroute to Germany.  He was honorably discharged in 1956 as Airman First Class. Bob married Yvonne (Martin) on December 15, 1956, and together they enjoyed nearly 70 years of marriage, raising two children, Denise and Craig. Bob worked for the Chrysler Proving Grounds in Chelsea as a driver/mechanic, and then in the Wind Tunnel, from 1956 until he retired in 1987. Bob and Yvonne traveled extensively across the United States, settling in southern Texas as Snowbirds for 24 years. He enjoyed being outdoors, hunting, fishing, and snowmobiling. He was an avid woodcarver, in Texas as well as with the Chelsea Senior Center woodcarving group. In addition to his wife, Yvonne, Bob is survived by a daughter, Denise A. Wirtz of Chelsea, MI, and son, Craig Wirtz of Honor, MI. Bob will be cremated, and a private graveside service will be held at Champion Hill Cemetery in Honor, Michigan next spring. Those wishing to make a memorial contribution in honor of Bob, may do so to the Chelsea Senior Center, with donations directed to Ease the Day Program, a structured caregiver respite program designed to give caregivers a break while providing meaningful engagement for older adults. title: East High to play in Section V Class B Football Championship following investigation into fight - WHEC.com

ROCHESTER, N.Y. — Section V confirmed that East High School will play in the Class B Football Sectional Championship following an investigation into a fight that broke out during the Class B semifinal. Video from viewer Tyler Colbey and News10NBC’s Ian Mills showed players from East High and Monroe High School throwing punches and wrestling each other to the ground during the semifinal game Saturday, Nov. 7. WATCH: Monroe and East players fight at high school football game in Rochester, RCSD investigates In a statement on the Section V website, it says a number of East High students were “misidentified as a disqualified player.” Therefore, East High will face Honeoye Falls-Lima on Saturday, Nov. 14 at 3:00 p.m. at St. John Fisher University. Section V said any student-athlete who was actually determined to be disqualified “remains subject to the required suspension of the next two consecutive halves of competition.” We’re still working to learn how many students were disqualified. Here’s the full statement Section V issued Wednesday: “Following a thorough investigation conducted by the Rochester City School District administration, and subsequent review by Section V and NYSPHSAA leadership, it has been determined that a number of East High School student-athletes were misidentified as a disqualified player following the Section V Class B football semifinal on Saturday, November 7. This determination was made following the submission and review of clear and compelling evidence in accordance with NYSPHSAA rules and regulations. Section V appreciates the Rochester City School District administration’s prompt and thorough efforts to investigate the incident and provide the necessary documentation to ensure an accurate and appropriate resolution. In accordance with the NYSPHSAA Sportsmanship Rule, any student-athlete determined to have been disqualified remains subject to the required suspension of the next two consecutive halves of competition. Following the completion of this review, Section V confirms that the Class B Football Sectional Championship between East High School and Honeoye Falls-Lima will proceed as scheduled on Saturday, November 14, at 3:00 PM at St. John Fisher University.” Rochester City School District Superintendent Dr. Eric Jay Rosser also issued the following statement: “I am pleased to share that our East High School student-athletes who were not involved in Saturday’s incident will have the opportunity to continue their season and compete in this Saturday’s Section V championship game. Since Saturday, our District leadership team and I have worked closely with Section V and the New York State Public High School Athletic Association to ensure our students received fair consideration. We are grateful to both organizations for their partnership, their willingness to review the evidence, and their commitment to ensuring that students who were not involved have the opportunity to continue their season. I also want to recognize our District athletics staff, who worked diligently to review video footage and photographs and provide the information necessary to support this process. Their dedication reflects our shared commitment to doing what is right for students. These young athletes have worked hard all season to earn this opportunity, and I could not be more pleased that they will have the chance to take the field on Saturday. We know how much this means to them, their coaches, their families, and our school communities. We appreciate the many members of our community who expressed their concern and support throughout this process. This outcome reflects what we can accomplish when we work together and keep students at the center of our decisions. I look forward to seeing our student-athletes back on the field Saturday and wish them the very best as they compete for the sectional championship.” RCSD and Section V started investigating what happened and what led up to the fight Sunday after the game. title: Sue V. Forrester - Rappahannock Record
content: ALFONSO—Sue Varney Forrester, a devoted educator, loving wife, and mother, and most dear to her heart, a cherished Nannie, passed away on November 3, 2026, leaving behind a legacy of love, patience, kindness and a deep love for animals. Born on May 13, 1952, in Logan, West Virginia, to Claude and Lois Varney, Sue lived a life centered around family, compassion and service to others. She married her Ronald Forrester, who preceded her in death earlier this past March. Sue leaves behind her loving children, Dwight and Amy Forrester, Charlotte and Aleksey Mironov, and Chad Forrester; her beloved grandchildren, Grafton and Sara Forrester, and Anton, Alina and Sully Mironov; her brothers, Gary (Karen) Varney and David (Sue) Varney; along with many cherished nieces and nephews. Throughout her life, Sue devoted herself to education, touching countless lives throughout Lancaster Public Schools. She believed education was about so much more than books and lessons. It was about building confidence, inspiring dreams, encouraging curiosity, and giving others the tools to reach their fullest potential. Perhaps her most treasured role was being Nannie. Her grandchildren were the light of her life, and she took great joy in loving them, cheering them on, and making memories they will carry in their hearts forever. Services will be held at 11 a.m. Saturday, November 14, at Lebanon Baptist Church in Alfonso. In lieu of flowers, memorial donations may be made to the Lancaster County Virginia Education Foundation or the Animal Welfare League of the Northern Neck. Currie Funeral Home LLC of Kilmarnock handled the arrangements.

title: Why ‘St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy’ Could Mark a Huge Win for Religious Freedom - Christianity Today
content: Advancing the stories and ideas of the kingdom of God. A Supreme Court case centering on a Catholic preschool could overturn nearly 40 years of precedent. The U.S. Supreme Court Building on October 05, 2026 in Washington, DC. The US Supreme Court heard a case last week that could shape the future of religious freedom in America. And if the justices’ questions were any indication, the court looks poised to deliver more robust protections for religious exercise while potentially discarding a nearly four-decade-old precedent in the process. The case, St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy, is straightforward. Colorado’s universal preschool program provides free preschool to children. To participate in the program, providers—both public and private—must sign a nondiscrimination agreement, requiring them to enroll students regardless of the sexual orientation and gender identity of students and their families. Some private religious providers objected to this requirement, arguing that enrolling children of same-sex couples could upset the religious environment of their schools. Colorado disagreed, claiming it should not be required to exempt religious schools from this requirement for public benefits. To more fully understand the stakes of this case, we must go back to 1990, when the court decided Employment Division v. Smith. In that case, the court held that if a law that ends up burdening religion is both neutral and generally applicable—that is, it applies to everybody and doesn’t target religion—then states are not obligated to grant religious exemptions from that law. Smith was a departure from an earlier decision, Sherbert v. Verner, in which the court said that a state could only burden religion if it had a compelling interest in doing so. During last week’s oral argument, several justices expressed skepticism about Colorado’s nondiscrimination requirement. Justice Samuel Alito highlighted several recent decisions at the intersection of religious freedom and LGBTQ rights, pointing out these precedents support the parish’s exemption request. Justice Amy Coney Barrett asked whether there was sufficient evidence of discrimination against LGBTQ families to warrant Colorado’s blanket policy precluding St. Mary’s from state funding. Justice Brett Kavanaugh, meanwhile, referenced the court’s past efforts to balance these sorts of questions: One of the things that Obergefell and Masterpiece were very careful to say, though, that in recognizing a constitutional right to same-sex marriage, that the court was also respecting the rights of people, particularly religious people who had religious beliefs that were different, and that it was important going forward as a country to make sure both rights were respected. Still, a few justices had concerns with St. Mary’s position. “Your bottom line,” Justice Sonya Sotomayor asked Nicholas Reaves, the parish’s attorney, “is your school can reject a child because their parents are homosexual?” She later wondered whether, under St. Mary’s position, a school could deny a student based on race or ethnicity. Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson was similarly concerned, questioning how this case would align with the diverse nature of American democracy: I understand you’re trying to move Smith to the side, but it had some really serious concerns about religious entities not having to follow the law that everybody else is just because they hold sincerely held religious beliefs. It was like, how are you going to have a society where all people live and work together? Importantly, some justices questioned whether Smith’s general applicability standard should remain the standard for free exercise cases. Justice Neil Gorsuch pondered whether Smith has already been effectively annulled via federal and state renditions of the Religious Freedom Restoration Act. And Justice Elena Kagan asked Reaves directly whether Smith should control this case (and future ones), or whether the court should rely on cases that “look at the burden on religion from the perspective of the religious believer,” a la Sherbert. In her reading of last week’s oral argument, law professor Stephanie Barclay predicted another recent decision may end up holding the answer to the present case. In 2022, the court handed down its decision in Carson v. Makin, ruling for families who wanted to send their children to sectarian schools using state funding. “A win under Carson,” Barclay wrote, “would be far more durable [than one under Smith]. It would hold that conditioning a public benefit on abandoning religious exercise triggers strict scrutiny, however the condition is drafted.” Triggering strict scrutiny—the most demanding standard of judicial review—requires the state to prove that its law or policy serves a compelling state interest, a high bar for government to meet. Based on last week’s oral argument, there appear to be at least five—and likely six—justices poised to side with St. Mary Catholic Parish. The bigger question, then, is how the court will decide this case. Will the justices continue to diminish the Smith precedent, or even formally overturn it? Or will they strike a balance between Smith and Carson, leaving the older precedent in place while nodding to their more recent decision? While the outcome of this case may appeal to some Christians more than others, the precedent it could set would be a win for everyone hoping for more robust protections for religious freedom. This might not settle questions at the heart of competing legal interests, but it would mark a return to a more faithful reading of what the First Amendment was supposed to accomplish in the first place—namely, protecting religious exercise, not just beliefs.
